extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, patent litigators, and USPTO examiners working on design patents
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing whether a claimed design is obvious under the Federal Circuit’s new LKQ framework, i.e., applying adapted Graham factors, analogous-art limits, and an overall-visual-impression inquiry for design patents. Useful for courts, PTAB decisions, and USPTO examination of design-patent validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rosen‑Durling test (historical standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior Federal Circuit framework requiring (1) a single prior art reference with 'basically the same' design characteristics as the claimed design (Rosen), and (2) any secondary references had to be 'so related' to the primary reference that 'the appearance of certain ornamental features in one would suggest the application of those features to the other' (Durling). If no Rosen reference existed, the obviousness inquiry would end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why the 'basically the same' threshold and 'so related' requirement made the prior analysis rigid; LKQ en banc rejects reliance on that categorical stopping rule. Example: Board in LKQ applied Rosen‑Durling and stopped when no Rosen reference was found.

rubrics_metrics.name: KSR flexible/common‑sense approach applied to design patents
rubrics_metrics.description: KSR's rejection of rigid 'teaching, suggestion, or motivation' (TSM) rules and endorsement of a more flexible, common‑sense obviousness inquiry should guide design‑patent obviousness as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal Circuit held KSR's broad principles for utility patents apply to design patents too — obviousness analysis 'cannot be confined by a formalistic conception.' LKQ extends KSR's flexible approach to design patents and rejects rigid formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply the Graham factors to design patents
rubrics_metrics.description: The traditional four Graham factors (scope and content of the prior art, differences between the prior art and the claimed invention, the level of ordinary skill in the art, and secondary considerations) apply to design‑patent obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court evaluated design patent obviousness by applying these factors in design context (e.g., Whitman Saddle). The Federal Circuit reaffirmed these factors and described how they map to design issues (see other rubric entries for specific mappings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and content of prior art: analogous art requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art considered in the Graham first factor should be limited to 'analogous art' — typically art in the same field of endeavor as the claimed design's article of manufacture, but it need not be literally in the same field if it is nevertheless analogous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court stated '[t]he primary reference will typically be in the same field of endeavor as the claimed ornamental design’s article of manufacture, but it need not be, so long as it is analogous art.' The opinion left open precise tests for analogy; USPTO guidance instructs examiners to consider analogous art when assessing prior art scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall visual impression — compare the claimed design as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness analysis focuses on the claimed design’s overall visual impression and not merely on selected individual features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit emphasized evaluating the visual impression 'as a whole' from the perspective of an ordinary designer/ordinary observer. Examples: LKQ directed attention to whether differences in certain visual features affected the overall impression so as to make designs not 'substantially the same.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess differences by their effect on overall visual impression
rubrics_metrics.description: When comparing prior art and the claimed design, courts should evaluate differences based on how they affect the overall visual appearance, rather than using a binary 'basically the same' test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board in LKQ found that differences between certain visual features affected overall visual impression. Under LKQ, differences must be analyzed to determine their impact on the overall impression from the viewpoint of an ordinary designer/observer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordinary designer / ordinary observer perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim should be assessed through the viewpoint of an ordinary designer (in determining obviousness) or ordinary observer (in anticipation/infringement/visual similarity inquiries), i.e., a person of ordinary skill in the pertinent design art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court explained that in design contexts the level of skill should be the 'ordinary designer in the field' and quoted the Gorham 'ordinary observer' standard ('if in the eye of an ordinary observer...') used to determine substantial similarity and deception. Whitman Saddle and LKQ applied these concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary considerations (objective indicia) apply to design patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary considerations such as commercial success, industry praise, and copying are relevant and apply equally in the obviousness analysis for design patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: LKQ affirmed that existing precedent regarding secondary considerations of non‑obviousness apply and should be considered as part of the Graham framework to rebut obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible use of primary and secondary references (analogous, not 'so related')
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary and secondary references can both be considered even if they are not 'so related' to each other; they must simply be analogous to the claimed design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike Durling (which required secondary references to be 'so related' to a primary reference), LKQ allows combination of references that are each analogous to the claimed design — broadening the scope of prior art that can be combined to show obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation to combine — need not be explicit in references but must be established without hindsight
rubrics_metrics.description: The motivation to combine prior-art references no longer needs to come from the references themselves (TSM), but some basis for combining must be established in the record and must not rely on hindsight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Following KSR principles, the court held that motivation can be shown by common-sense reasoning and other evidence; however, courts and factfinders must ensure motivation is in the record and do not reconstruct combinations using hindsight bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordinary evidentiary standard and remand for application
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts should apply the flexible, fact‑based test case‑by‑case; where prior decisions used rigid tests, factfinders must reevaluate under the LKQ framework and may need remands to apply the new framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: LKQ remanded to the Board to apply the new framework. The opinion recognized that a flexible fact‑based test is more challenging but is manageable; the USPTO issued examiner guidance and plans further training.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO examiner guidance: assess overall visual impression and motivation to modify prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO examiners are instructed to assess design‑patent obviousness based on the overall visual impression and the motivation to modify prior art while considering analogous art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USPTO Director Vidal's memo (May 22, 2024) directed examiners to implement the LKQ test, to consider analogous art and motivation to modify, and to expect further USPTO guidance and training.
